content.title: Artemis II splashdown in California visual guide, what it would look like
content.text: April 9, 2026, 2:17 p.m. ETLive coverage of NASA's Artemis II splashdown in California, including livestream and updates, will be at floridatoday.com/space.Millions watched Artemis II launch from NASA's Kennedy Space Center, Florida. Can people in California see the Orion capsule splashdown?When SpaceX Dragon Endurance spacecraft landed off the coast of Tampa, Florida, in 2023, it left a streak in the sky.When NASA's SpaceX Crew-6 returned for splashdown off the coast of Jacksonville, Florida, in 2023, the capsule left a streak over Kennedy Space Center.When there’s a rocket launch, people tend to see a streak in the sky.When there’s a space-related splashdown, it also looks like a streak in the sky − and a water rescue.Last week, the world tuned in April 1, 2026, as NASA launched its Space Launch System rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, sending four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon.The most important leg of the historic moon mission was completed April 6 after the four astronauts spent hours making observations of the moon's far side, which is permanently faced away from Earth. The close approach, known as a lunar flyby, was a trailblazing moment in spaceflight, taking astronauts Reid Wiseman, Christina Koch and Victor Glover of NASA, as well as Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency, the farthest any human has been from Earth.NASA, space enthusiasts and news media from around the world, including the USA TODAY Network, have documented everything, from the picturesque liftoff in Florida, to the incredible lunar flyby, to a jar of Nutella floating in the Orion capsule.And now, the Artemis II astronauts are on their way home and preparing for a water landing off the coast of California, leaving the moon in the rearview mirror after becoming the first humans in more than 50 years to travel near Earth's celestial neighbor.But what does splashdown look like? Keep reading.Where will NASA Artemis II splashdown in California? See Artemis II landing visibility mapWhen is NASA Artemis II splashdown in California? See countdown clockThe Artemis II astronauts' Orion capsule is scheduled to splash down at about 8:07 p.m. ET Friday, April 10, 2026, off the coast of San Diego, California. The USA TODAY Network will have a livestream and live coverage at floridatoday.com/space.1. Splashdown begins.The astronauts are heading back to Earth, using our planet's gravity to naturally "slingshot," or pull Orion back home, negating the need for propulsion or much fuel.Just as a rocket launch has that definitive streak, the capsule heading toward the ocean for splashdown tends to leave a trail in the sky. It's particularly easier to see (and capture with photos or video) when splashdown occurs in the evening or early morning. And like a rocket launch, sometimes splashdown is visible far beyond its intended landing point. Examples of that are below.2. Parachutes deploy.First, two smaller drogue parachutes that are 23 feet in diameter will unfurl at an altitude of 25,000 feet to slow the capsule from about 25,000 mph to 307 mph, according to NASA. Next, three small 11-foot-wide auxiliary parachutes, known as pilot chutes, will be used at about 9,500 feet to ultimately make way for the release of the final three main parachutes.Those giant 116-foot-wide main parachutes are to slow Orion from about 130 mph to just 17 mph before the spacecraft lands in the Pacific Ocean.A photo below shows the "parachute portion" of splashdown for the Apollo 17 spacecraft off the coast of American Samoa (midway between Hawaii and New Zealand) in 1972.After the Artemis I launch in November 2022 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida, which had no astronauts aboard, the Orion capsule splashed down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California.The photos below show what the deployed parachutes look like from previous splashdowns − day, night and more than 50 years ago during NASA's Apollo program.3. Airbags deploy.After the Artemis II astronauts drift toward the ocean for an estimated 8:07 p.m. ET Friday, April 10, 2026, parachute-assisted water landing, the Orion capsule holding them will splash down in the Pacific Ocean near the coast of San Diego, California. Then, five orange airbags will inflate around the top of the spacecraft and flip the capsule into an upright position, making the exit easier for recovery crews.4. Artemis II recoveryAfter the landing, the crew would exit the vehicle onto the U.S. Navy recovery vessel within about two hours.If the Pacific Ocean conditions are particularly rough, they could pause recovery options until the waters calm down. The photo below shows the Amentum recovery team and how many people are involved in safely retrieving the Artemis II crew.5. Getting the Artemis II astronauts out of the Orion capsuleOnce the astronauts splash down, it's the Department of War's job, together with NASA's Johnson Space Center to get the astronauts out of the Orion capsule.A "stabilizing collar" put around the crew module helps keep the Orion spacecraft floating upright in the water. Once stable, teams will install a large inflatable “front porch." The personnel get the astronauts out of the Orion spacecraft and safely onto this floating platform. Each Artemis II crew member will be hoisted up into a helicopter basket for transport to the naval vessel. Then they'll get an evaluation at a medical bay before being taken back to NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.Watch rocket launches, live California splashdown coverage with NASA+ on Prime VideoWatch NASA+ content with Amazon Prime VideoNASA content, including some rocket launches and the Artemis II splashdown off the coast of California, is available to watch through NASA+ on desktop, both from its official site and YouTube. The platform is also available to download as a mobile app on smartphones.All NASA+ content is also available to those who have Prime Video downloaded on any of their devices – whether it be a smartphone or smart TV.Contributing: Lianna Norman and Kim Luciani, USA TODAY Network, Rick Neale, FLORIDA TODAYSangalang is a lead digital producer for USA TODAY Network. Follow her on Twitter or Instagram at @byjensangalang. Support local journalism. Subscribe to the free Florida TODAY newsletter.Eric Lagatta is the Space Connect reporter for the USA TODAY Network.
